Hi all, I'm a content creator on youtube but found myself in kind of a jam. When GamerGate got underway I jumped on the bandwagon there and started using #GamerGate to garner more views for the new podcast I was running. However it was always sort of awkward as a good chunk of the time we'd wander onto random subjects that had nothing to do with GamerGate and really, the point was to simply have interesting people onto talk who I happened to find on GG groups. So I've recently started, as the point isn't really about GamerGate, to stop using the hashtag.

This has put me in a jam however. As I said the contributors I pick up all come from GamerGate. As an individual, I myself am still a strong supporter and even if I wasn't I really do try and create content about the state of internet journalism (of which Gaming Press is a huge subsection,) idiots who slander, and basically content that appeals to the GamerGate audience. I can't go neutral because GamerGaters will obviously express support when they are on my show and I don't nearly have the numbers of TB to exactly not suckle off of opportunities like using the #GamerGate hashtag. Still, I want to keep reaching people who are interested.

Basically, my question is this: Is there any other way than using a hashtag, or some other hashtag, to reach people? I don't want to be the idiot who sends those dumb twitter messages to any random person who follows my channel's feed, but I don't really know of any other way.

As always, thank you for your time.

No matter if you use Notepad, Eclipse, Visual Studio, Emacs, Dreamweaver, or Frontpage there has to be something you hate about it and find annoying.

So lets hear it.
Most Annoying Thing About a Tool

Something that pissed me off pretty much right away was how different dev "houses" reimplement similar functionality. This isn't so much a tool problem, but an ecosystem problem.

For example, if I understand C/C++ I probably have a good grasp of what a primitive data type is. Sure, there's the whole architecture dependence, but we tend to have 16-bit integers (int), 8-bit characters (char), and so on. Well, along comes this one company standardized this nonsense of using WORD, DWORD, QWORD, and so on. Sure, it's not overly complex, but it serves no purpose other than to call a thing something else. Fuck's sake.
Reminds me of diagramming in Visio: Oh, you want to pick a datatype for your attribute? Please choose from this list of 10,000 data types.
Exactly. The whole thing is just bullshit. I understand inventing terms for branding and such, but shit like this just makes development slower and more tedious.

I have a ton but one that still drives me nuts in Visual Studio: Docking of windows.

I know, I know, docking in VS2010+ is super easy compared to the past but you can still manage to create a mess fast. Say you accidently undock the Solution Explorer window. It's a critical window and by default in an ideal place, so you try to put it back and by accident you dock it in the Properties area.

Oops.

You try to undock it from the Properties area but you are now undocking the entire bottom window which used to be just the Properties window but now has the Solution Explorer AND the Properties window attached. While trying to undo your undock because you see the mistake already, it snaps into the upper container and you just lost the stackable containers. Now have one tall and narrow container with 5 tabs.

You silently say to yourself, "I can work with it like this. It's not bad." Deep down inside you know you can't and this frustrates you.

Angrily you pull out the Properties window and try to dock it back below and it doesn't allow you to snap below because that container has since disappeared. It snaps to the Output/Error List area instead.

You scream and throw your coffee mug at the intern. He looks confused but you didn't hit him so it's cool.

While trying to pull the Properties window out of the Error List container area you instead undock the entire container like you did before. Ultimately you now have one tall and skinny window with 25 tabs and nowhere to dock any of them.

You pause for a moment and assess the situation.

Ultimately decide to reformat your hard drive so you can reinstall Visual Studio and get your stacked windows back. True story
They put Find All References too close to Go To Definition. I use both of them a lot, and I'm often in for a long wait if I hit FAR accidentally.
Oh. And let me stop the program while you're still building, VS! I don't want to wait 30 to 60 seconds when I realized I missed something two seconds after hitting run.
